newsitem.title: UK: West criticises Serbia ahead of Bosnia conference.
newsitem.headline: West criticises Serbia ahead of Bosnia conference.

text.p: Western countries on Monday gave Belgrade a foretaste of what is to come at a Bosnia conference this week by criticising a threat to crack down on protesters challenging Serbian President Slobodan Milosevic.
Serbian police threatened on Sunday to take firm measures against demonstrators who have marched in their thousands over the past two weeks to challenge Milosevic's rule.
Britain and France called on Monday for calm and said they were disturbed by talk of a crackdown.
International peace mediator Carl Bildt called on Milosevic to drop the idea of suppressing the protests and said Serbia had to adopt radical democratic reforms,
A senior U.S. official said there could not be a "decent peace in the Balkans" unless Serbia became an open and democratic society.

Milosevic and Croatian President Franjo Tudjman will not attend the Peace Implementation Conference on Wednesday and Thursday, due to take stock of the Bosnian peace process which started when the Dayton peace treaty was signed a year ago.
Milosevic and Tujdman, who is also facing protests against his rule, are sending their foreign ministers instead.

"Whereas in Dayton the support of Milosevic and Tudjman was seen as essential for supporting the shaky peace deal, their democratic credentials are now under increasing scrutiny," said a Western diplomat closely involved in the Dayton process.
"What they will hear now is some sharp criticism -- there will be no plaudits here for them."
Tudjman, reported to be ill with cancer, faces criticism for suppressing the independent media. He failed last month in a bid to close down a popular independent radio station.

Thousands of Serbs protested after Milosevic's ruling party reversed a stunning defeat in November local elections and annulled unfavourable results in 15 of the biggest Serbian cities, including the capital Belgrade.
"Milosevic is behaving as though Serbia has decided to align itself not with Europe but with the few remaining dictatorships in the world," the diplomat said.
Milosevic raised the stakes over the weekend when the police said they would no longer tolerate street protests.
"All this is likely to wreck any discussion on restoring Serbia's ties with the International Monetary Fund," the diplomat said.

Veteran Western observers in Belgrade believe that Milosevic is trying to wear down the opposition and hoping the West will overlook the domestic turmoil in return for his continuing commitment to the Bosnia peace.
Both Milosevic and Tudjman were hailed as peacemakers for their role during the Dayton talks.
"Presumably Milosevic thought this gave him carte blanche to do whatever he wanted at home," the diplomat said.
"On the contrary, the election issue will now become a condition for Serbia's reintegration into the world."
A senior U.S. official, who asked not to be identified, said Washington acknowledged "the nature of the regime" despite Milosevic's important role in the Dayton process.

"While President Milosevic and Serbia were an integral part of those negotiations...we believe that there cannot be a decent peace in the Balkans without an open and prosperous and democratic Serbia," the official said.
